A SHARP ENGAGEMENT IN "COWTOWN."

The poundmen got another warm reception this morning, this time in Cowtown, just above Boundary street. About 5 o'clock Poundmaster Einstein and his men, accompanied by Policeman Farquhar, paid a visit to this usually quiet "burg" and surrounded fifteen dogs. Before they could get them into the wagon the natives drove the dogs away. The poundmen then turned their attention to a flock of geese in a neighboring creek. The female inhabitants seemed to have a special interest in the geese, and they turned out in force, armed with paving stones, sticks and table-knives. The men, inspired by the presence and daring of the women, combined forces with them and made a very effective assault, the poundmen retreating in good order after taking one prisoner—Patrick Murphy. During the fight Murphy struck one of the poundmen on the head with a large stone, and one of the women cut the tail nearly off Gen. Einstein's coat with a table-knife. John Keeefe was arrested for profanity, and David Nelligan for disorderly conduct. The police are on the track of a number of others whom they expect to arrest. In the Police Court to-day Murphy's counsel had his case continued until Monday to get witnesses. Keeefe's case was also continued, and Nelligan forfeited collateral.
albert-fortune-washington-1882-08-19.A2:
The War in Cowtown.
Jno. Keefe, who was before the Police Court last Saturday in connection with the assault on the poundmaster and his men in "Cowtown," whose case was continued for evidence for the defense, was before the court again this morning, charged with cursing and swearing. Mr. P. B. Stillson appeared for the prisoner. Mr. Einstein testified that about 6 o'clock last Saturday morning he and his assistants and Policeman Farquhar paid a visit to the neighborhood mentioned and surrounded 15 dogs and a flock of geese, and were attacked by a large crowd of men and women, and the dogs and geese were driven off; that Albert Fortune, one of the witness' colored assistants, was struck on the head with a large stone thrown by a young man named Patrick Murphy, who retreated into a cornfield, and when followed by witness, the officer, and his men, Jno. Keefe came out and called for a gun, so that he could "kill the niggers," and cursed and swore. This statement was corroborated by the policeman and the colored men. Testimony was heard for the defense, after which the court fined the defendant $2 or 7 days. Maggie Long, the daughter of Mr. Keefe, and her husband, Patrick H. Long, were then charged with obstructing the poundmaster while in the discharge of his duty. The charge against Maggie, a young woman, was first tried. The testimony of the poundmaster and his men was to the effect that she armed herself with a large stone and had to be disarmed several times, and that she was the leader of the crowd. A fine of $5 or 15 days was imposed in this case. A charge of assault was then tried against Patrick Murphy, who was charged with striking Albert Dodson, one of the colored poundmen, on the head with a stone. Several witnesses testified for the defense that Murphy was assaulted by one of the colored poundmen. The prisoner said he has no geese, and his dog wears a tag, and he was only a spectator. The court, after hearing other testimony, imposed a fine of $5 or 15 days in this case. An appeal was noted.
albert-fortune-washington-1882-08-19.A3:
Pounding the Poundmen.
In the Police Court yesterday the mob attack on the Poundmaster by the residents of the vicinity of Sherman avenue on Saturday was investigated, and the evidence, which confirmed what has already been published, resulted in the following action by the court: John Keeefe was charged with ordering the poundmen out of a cornfield, and saying he would get a gun and chase the "—— niggers off the hill." A two-dollar fine was imposed for profanity. Mrs. Maggie Long was charged with obstructing the poundmen and endeavoring to pelt them with stones. Judge Bundy said that the defendant being a woman he would be content with a five-dollar fine. Patrick Murphy, a young white man, was charged with striking Albert Fortune, one of the poundmen, on the back of the head with a stone, and was fined $5.

Mr. James Townsend, who, with his son, Mr. W. C. Townsend, has been planting rice at the LeConte place, in the lower portion of Liberty county, lost his barn and commissary by fire one night last week. Sneak thieves are walking off with cotton in Dublin.

The project of a cotton seed oil mill has been broached in Dublin.

Andrew Rivers, charged with the murder of Mrs. J. M. Clews and child, in Thomas county, a few months ago, has escaped from Valdosta jail, whither he was sent for safe keeping. It is thought he had help from outside.

The Griffin News learns that James F. White, who so cruelly shot Mr. James Rose, in Upson county, some weeks ago, has been captured, and will be speedily brought to justice. He was apprehended in Mobile county, Ala.

The Albany News and Advertiser reports that during the high wind of Saturday afternoon, a whirlwind struck a log cabin on Mr. Croff Mayo's Huger place, the sole occupant of which was Tom Lee, a negro blacksmith. A sill fell across his abdomen, and he died in two hours after being extricated from the debris. He was about fifty-five years of age, and had been in Mr. Mayo's employment some years. He had his leg amputated a few years ago.

The Augusta Evening News states that a little negro boy, Allen Moore, was committed by Recorder Webb Tuesday morning to await the action of the grand jury in a curious case of killing. Last May Allen was fighting with another small negro named Robert Griffin and struck the latter on the head with a brick. Griffin died three weeks since and the little fellow who caused his death is now committed for trial. He cannot be more than thirteen years of age and his parents say he is only ten.

Orange Law, a respectable colored man living near Riceboro, in Liberty county, had some money. Not having any confidence in banks since the days of the Freedman's Bank, he put his money in a trunk and hid the trunk under the shucks in his crib. Some one got the key of the crib to get some harness. Now Orange Law mourns the loss of his trunk and $315 in cash.

Sip Williams and Dublin Maberry, young gentlemen of color, are in Louisville jail regretting the fact that they tried their hand at burglary only to be caught.

Three Suspected House Burners in Peril in Lincoln County.
AUGUSTA, January 30 —There is considerable excitement in Lincoln county lately growing out of an attempt to burn the residence of P. A. Cox, within four miles of Lincolnton. cowboy-cochise-county-1882-04.A1: LIFE IN ARIZONA.—Trouble and loss are still caused by the cow boys in Cachise county, Arizona. The mules and work oxen at Major Downing's sawmill, twenty miles distant, were stolen six weeks ago. Since then a cowboy has been lynched near there, after having confessed, it is said, that he was the thief. Mr. White, a ranchman thirty miles south, had all his vaquero stock run off recently. In this camp a good horse cannot be kept without watching. If we were living under some petty European Government that did not to pretend to protect its subjects against the raid of thieves, we might not be surprised at the position in which we find ourselves.—Correspondent of the San Francisco Bulletin.

According to the Virginia (New) Chronicle, the Government bonds, amounting to $7100, which the late John L. Moore of that city willed to his daughter, were found recently by J. W. Howard, his son-in-law, and Joseph Josephs. They were in a tin box, secreted in the attic of the old man's house, between the ceiling and the roof. Logan Leader: We learn of the very sad accident which occurred to Mr. Samuel Handy of Franklin on Sunday the 15th. A pair of his horses had broken loose and Mr. Handy mounted a young horse, and started after the runaway which he headed off about a mile from his house. He was seen coming back with them by his wife through the window. Soon after the three horses were seen by Mrs. Handy coming into the yard together. She wondered at this but supposed her husband had stopped on the way. As Mr. Handy did not return the wife instituted a search for him, when his dead body was found across the wagon road. The remaines were at once taken to the home of the deceased. An inquest was held before Justice Webster, and a verdict rendered to the effect that the deceased met with his death by falling from a horse and breaking his neck.

S. L. Tribune: Friday night when the treasurer of the Oates troup counted up the receipts of the house, he was somewhat taken aback at running across a bogns dollar. He hailed the door keeper, and showing him the money remarked that it was first time in all his nine years' experience with shows that he had ever been bitten with a counterfeit silver piece. Gold and greenbacks had at times gotten largely the best of him, but silver, never. Then he continued his count, and presently struck another, and another, and then he began to indulge in a regular typhoon of theatrical profanity. As the count continued the bogus dollars kept showing up a strong force until, lo and behold, there was just $75 in bogus coin that had been dumped into the opera bouffe exchequer. The probabilities are that everybody who found bogus dollars on their hands concluded that the shortest route to redemption was to patronize the theatre. Some probably thought that the counterfeit money was a stand-off for some of the padded calves in the chorus. In settling up accounts the local managers shouldered half the loss.

Ogden Pilot: Mrs Fred Nichols of Eagle Rock, met with a sad accident last week, while carrying a bucket of water, by falling across the bucket, fracturing the thigh bone and breaking some of her ribs. In the absence of a physician she had to be sent to Logan for treatment but her recovery is doubtful.

Invitations are out for another one of those enjoyable parties given by Mr. and Mrs. Clifford of Eagle Rock, for next Tuesday evening.

The Las Animas (Col.) Leader reports that an extensive prairie fire was raging last week between Butte and Bear creeks. It traveled about twenty miles a day and the flames were running high.

On Saturday last while the emigrant train of the Union Pacific Railroad was near Wasatch Station, a young girl, a passenger, named Nina Collins, stepped out onto one of the flat cars, when a sudden jerk of the train threw her off her feet, and falling between the cars, the coaches running over both legs above the knees, crushing them in a horrible manner. She was taken to Rawlins where her legs were amputated, but she only lived thirty-six hours. On the same day a brakesman named Jas. Brandolph while the train was near Filmore Station, stepped from one of the cars and fell under the wheels and was run over both legs being severed from the body at the groin. Evening News: By D. K. Reid of Castle Dale, Emery County, we are informed of the killing, on the 21st inst., of William Nugent, known as "California Bill," by William Duffy. The tragedy occurred at Blake City. The two had quarreled during the day, Duffy getting the worst of the fight. He subsequently procured a Winchester rifle with which he shot Nugent through the body, killing him. Nugent wounded Duffy in the calf of the leg, with a pistol shot. The affair raised quite an excitement, and threats of lynching Duffy were freely indulged in. This is the second homicide in Emery County within a very brief period, D. L. Blizzard being the previous victim.

February 10th, 1882.
Editors Herald:

Editors Herald:

I met a man in the canyon, today, on his way to Clear Creek, who claims to have been an eye witness to the shooting affray that took place at Green River on the 21st ult. From a short conversation with him I gleaned the following facts in relation to it: It appears that California Bill—whose right name is Wm. Neugent, from California—and Duffy were, in the phraseology of the place, "bunkeys," and shared the same bed; they were working for Neilson & Jensen, railroad contractors, east of Green River. On the day of the shooting they left camp together, quarreling all the way out over trivial matters; after they arrived in camp they indulged in several drinks together, but were by no means intoxicated, and quarreled again—over what I am unable to learn—and parted; but in a few minutes they returned, Bill with a pistol and Duffy with a rifle; as they met in front of Taylor's saloon, Bill fired on his former chum, the ball passing through the calf of his left leg; then Duffy raised his rifle and fired at Neugent, the ball entering his left breast and coming out under the shoulder blade; he fell backward through the doorway into the saloon and expired almost immediately. Duffy ran across the river, followed by a number of men, and after a short chase he was captured. It was only through the intercession of the cooler headed men that he escaped being lynched. He is now in the Provo Jail.

The people that constitute the better class of the population of this place are just awakening to the fact that a peaceable citizen's life will not be safe until some of the roughs that infest the country are made to perform the tight rope act and dance on nothing, for they continue to make things uncomfortably lively. On several occasions Mr. Forbs, who has charge of the D. and R. G. warehouse, has been run over the river at the muzzle of a gun by these playful scamps.

Two men were severely injured here on the 27th ult. They were working on the grade blasting rock; a blast was lighted, the fuse burned up, but the powder failed to ignite. They foolishly attempted to drill it out to save the powder, when it exploded, cutting them badly about the face and hands, one of them losing nearly the whole of his hand, and bruised their bodies considerably. They were sent to Salt Lake for repairs.

In Marseilles, the Crystal Palace theatre has been destroyed by fire. The loss is 1,000,000 francs. The actors had great difficulty in effecting their escape from the burning building.

In St. Petersburg a fire broke out in the Winter Livadia theatre during the performance. So far as known no lives were lost.

Setting Forests on Fire.

It is believed that the fires started in the woods at Mastic, in the town of Brookhaven, N. Y., and which destroyed over fifty acres of valuable timber, were started by oyster thieves. Evidence has been secured against several persons, and a number of arrests are expected in a few days. The woods and houses are now guarded night and day.

Snow Blockade.

The snow blockade on the Central Pacific railroad continues. Advices from Emigrant Gap say that a snow plow, with eight engines, has cleared the road between Truckee and Blue Canon. Two sections of a western bound emigrant train and two plows are stuck between Atla and Blue Canon. One section of a western-bound passenger train is also lying there. It is now snowing.

Last Saturday night, at Hudson, Wis., Mrs. George Miles shot her husband while he was attempting to enter her residence on lower Second street, inflicting a painful but not dangerous wound. It seems the domestic relations of the unhappy pair have not been delightful since their marriage some thirteen years ago, because he was shiftless and cranky and she was hardly economical enough with her virtue for a well regulated helpmate. James Ryan, a convict in the penitentiary a Stillwater, died Tuesday of consumption, and was buried in Fairview cemetery. Information About the Floods.

St. Louis, March 21.—The Clerk of the steamer City of Providence, just from Vicksburg, gives some information about the floods on the lower rivers not before published. He says the Parasol Steamboat Company, which runs steamers up the Yazoo river and its tributaries, is doing more to assist and rescue the people in that district than the Government and everybody else combined. It has sent into the submerged district of the Yazoo river, the Sunflower and the Tallahassee, the light-draft steamers Desmet and Headlight, equipped for special work. Each boat is supplied with a full complement of skiffs, axes and other necessary utensils. They steam into the flood as far as practicable, then anchor and send detachments in every direction to look for the sufferers. They have medicines, stimulants, etc., in each boat. The crews are started out in the morning, with instructions to prosecute their searches until nearly dark and then to return. The Sunflower, says the Clerk, returned the day he left Vicksburg. On board she had 350 sufferers, and her deck was crowded with cattle that had been picked up. The people on board were nearly all sick and a majority of them in destitute circumstances. Another of their boats, the Headlight, is expected back at any time. She will also be crowded with passengers and cattle. The worst point on the whole river is Milligan's Bend. There is an overflow and a counter overflow in that district. The waters from the Mississippi are going over the levee, and the floods and back-water from the Yazoo are coming in from behind. As a consequence where these two bodies meet a whirlpool is formed, which destroys everything in its course. The locality of the whirlpool is changing constantly, and every day it completes new destruction. A large yawl filled with negroes was caught in it the other day and upset, and all of the occupants drowned. The whirlpool struck a church a few days ago, in which several people with their stock had taken refuge. The church was in a few minutes torn to pieces, the stock was drowned and the people floated around in the water some hours, but were finally rescued. The vortex struck the residence and stable of an old paralytic farmer named Jameson, and totally annihilated them. The old gentleman was drowned.

WASHINGTON, March 21.—A bill was introduced in the House yesterday by Representative Cassidy to compel a survey of the lands embraced within railroad subsidy limits. It sets forth that more than 25,000,000 acres remain unsurveyed of lands granted to the Central Pacific, Union Pacific and Kansas Pacific Railways, and that these companies, by their failure to cause a survey to be made, evade taxes in the States and Territories in which they lie, the revenues to which they are justly entitled. PITTSBURG, September 21.—The differences between the manufacturers and iron workers having been settled, a large number of mills started up with a full complement of men today, and the balance will be in operation by next Monday. The best feeling exists between the employers and employees, and all sides appear to be glad that the strike is over. Fowley, who was a non-Union man, shot Critchlow, and has since been at work at the mill. When the Union men went to work this morning, in order to save trouble, Fowley resigned, and Manager Williams then discharged Critchlow. Negroes Lynched.
CHARLESTON (S. C.), June 12th.—The negro John Johnson, who outraged Miss McDowell at Rock Hill yesterday, was lynched this morning.
St. Louis, June 12th.—A special from Jackson, Miss., to the Post-Dispatch says: George Beckett, a negro, attempted to outrage the seven-year-old daughter of a man named Agnew, in Monroe county, yesterday. A party of citizens, with shotguns and blood-hounds, started in pursuit of the brute, and he was run down near Tombigbee river. He refused to surrender, and defied his pursuers, who opened fire on him, wounding him seriously. He was then taken to jail and a guard placed over him. At night a crowd overpowered the jailer, broke into Beckett's cell, dragged him out, and hanged him to the limb of a tree.

Murderers Lynched.
LAWRENCE (Ks.), June 12th.—Peter Vinegar, George Robinson and Ike King were taken from jail here Saturday morning at 1 o'clock by a crowd of vigilantes and hanged from the bridge. Robinson pleaded for his life, and fell on his knees three times. King said when he was about to drop, "Boys, let me down easy." The men behind him said, "Did you let Bandsman down easy?" and gave the plank a neck. The necks of Vinegar and Robinson were broken, that of King was not. There is talk of revenge on the part of the colored people, though most of them say the punishment was deserved.

Prize Fight near New York.
NEW YORK, June 12th.—Murray and Greene, the pugilists, fought this morning near Fort Hamilton. The latter was terribly punished, and lost the fight.

Another Prize Fight at Coney Island.
NEW YORK, June 12th.—Leonard Tracy and Alexander Brown fought fifty-seven rounds with bare fists at Coney Island yesterday, for $200 a side. The affair ended in a wrangle.

Mrs. Scoville's Petition.
CHICAGO, June 12th.—Mr. Scoville reports that the morning mail brought in over 600 signatures for her petition in behalf of her brother.

WASHINGTON, June 12th.—The Postoffice officials say the surplus of receipts over expenditures for the past year will foot up in the vicinity of $1,000,000.

The Dying Governor.
COLUMBUS (O.), June 12th.—Ex-Governor Dennison is gradually declining, and his death is looked for at any hour.

BOSTON, June 12th.—A brick building in Wareham street was burned this morning. Loss, $60,000; partly insured.
SAVANNAH (Ga.), June 12th.—The Savannah Cotton Seed Oil Mills, on Hutchinson Island, opposite the city, were burned this morning. Loss, $50,000; insurance, $28,000.
Graduating Day at West Point.
WEST POINT (N. Y.), June 12th.—The exercises attending graduating day at West Point Military Academy took place to-day. General Howard presented a diploma to each graduate as he responded to his name, being loudly applauded.
The Maine Republicans.
PORTLAND, June 12th.—The Republican Convention meets here to-morrow. The contest for Governor is narrowing to Thomas and Robie.
Wells' Comet.
ALBANY (N. Y.), June 12th.—A successful obervation of Wells' comet was made at the Dudley Observatory yesterday and today at the meridian transit. The most interesting fact ascertained is that this comet has a real nucleus.
Wind and Fire.
MOSCOW, June 12th.—A violent gale occurred here yesterday. The Exhibition building was greatly damaged. A fire broke out during the storm in the Ragosoki quarter, and 100 houses, mostly wood, were destroyed.

Another Balloon Project.
WASHINGTON, June 12th.—The project of crossing the Atlantic in a balloon has again been revived. A prominent Eastern astronaut proposes to cross the big water in an airship larger than any heretofore constructed, and supplied with a light but secure boat, which is to take the place of the usual wicker-work car. The cloth covering is to be of triple thickness, with a view both of preventing the escape of gas and of strengthening the balloon. Drags and water-anchors are to be used to assist in keeping the airship in the right direction, and also to prevent the boat from overturning. The cost of the outfit is placed at $15,000. It is proposed to start from the vicinity of Washington, where it is thought a current of air can be struck which will carry the balloon to the other side of the Atlantic.

Land Speculators Checkmated.

THE LAWRENCE LYNCHING.

LEAVENWORTH, Kas., June 12.—A special to The Standard from Lawrence says a large meeting of colored people was held there this evening in reference of the lynching of three negroes there on the 10th by a party of masked men. The men who were hung were King, Robertson and Vinegar, the first two for the murder of a white man ten days before, and the other as an accomplice. The whole town was in a state of intense excitement. The following resolution was passed, with others:

Resolved, That we recommend to the colored people of this city to abstain from all expressions tending to increase the present excitement in the public mind.

INDICTED.

All the iron manufacturers west of the Allegheny mountains, representing a capital of $35,000,000, gathered at Pittsburgh and resolved to stand firm against an advance in wages. The Superior rail mill, in Allegheny City, started up with a force of green hands, who ruined four tons of good material.

Five hundred head of cattle were poisoned by eating a noxious weed on a farm near Montreal, Canada, and a large number died. They were brought from the West en route to England.

A party of well-to-do Mississippi negroes are en route to Chihuahua, Mexico, for the purpose of prospecting the country. If they can secure property cheap they intend to establish a colony.

The body of Frank Small, who was executed at Pittsburg, Pa., on Friday, was put on exhibition by the aunt of the deceased. Twenty-five cents admission was charged to view the remains, and for seven hours a continuous stream of people gratified a horrible curiosity. The Mayor at last heard of the affair and ordered the police to take charge of the corpse. When they reached the scene nearly 10,000 people had gathered in the vicinity. About 5,000 of the assemblage followed Small's body to the grave.

Harry and Curtland Gordon were arrested on a charge of robbing and maltreating an aged couple at Vincennes, Ind. A mob tried to take them out of jail and hang them, but were baffled by a plucky Sheriff. They were tried a few days ago and found guilty. Thereupon their brother Joe declared himself and an uncle to be the guilty ones. He had intended to keep silent if his brother were acquitted, but would not let them go to state prison. He said that he was present at the attempted lynching, and would then have spoken out if it had been necessary.

Thriving Business of Judge Lynch.
On the 19th of December last, J. B. Weisinger, a plante, near Brown's station, Alabama, a man 60 years of age, was brutally murdered in his own house, half a dozen negroes being supposed to have had a hand in it. Two of them named Bill Ludlow and Al. Weisinger, were finally brought to trial and convicted, and on the 31st of March executed. On Wednesday of last week Henry Ivy, suffering under the pangs of conscience since the execution, made a voluntary confession to seven intelligent colored men to the effect that he and his brother, Porter Ivy, and another negro named Sim Acoff, had been parties to the murder of old man Weisinger, he himself (Henry Ivy) having really done the killing, though Porter Ivy and Sim Acoff, as well as the two men who were hanged, had been equally guilty participants. When this confession became generally known the negroes upon the plantation became furiously excited, and Ivy and Acoff who had meantime been arrested and bound over for their appearance before the grand jury, were taken in charge by three white men and placed in a school house for safe keeeping. At midnight, however, forty masked men, thoroughly armed, rode up to the building, quickly overcame and bound the guard, and rode off with the negroes. Next day the lifeless bodies of Ivy and Acoff were found in the road hanging from the limbs of two trees.

Three other victims of Judge Lynch are reported from Kerleyville, Mo. For some time past the people of that neighborhood were troubled by the depredations of horse-thieves. At length three men were discovered to be the ringleaders in the robberies. They were hunted down on the 14th inst. and taken to the pinery some distance from town and hung. The hanging was swiftly performed, and the vigilantes dispersed the moment the men were swung up. There was a good deal of excitement, as this was the first triple hanging that had occurred in that section of Missouri for several years. The names of the thieves are unknown. They were said to hail from Greene county, Missouri.

val spoon there was a very wide spread dissatisfaction on the part of the public with religious oyster stews. The truth is that the festival managers had been compelled to practice an economy in oysters to which the public mind and palate refused to be reconciled. The well-established rule in preparing stewed oysters for church festivals was that one oyster should be used with every quart of water, and that in serving customers a half of an oyster only should be given to each one. One quart of oysters, in accordance with this system, was expected to furnish sufficient food for one hundred people, and as the original quart rarely cost over fifty cents and each stew made from it was sold for thirty cents it followed that a clear profit of nearly thirty dollars could be made from every quart of oysters. Of course, where a church festival was attended by four or five hundred people the profits of the oyster department were very large, and, indeed, in most cases averaged double those of the ice cream department.

While this system was financially a brilliant success it was not satisfactory to hungry people. It was complained, and with some show of justice, that while an oyster stew ought to preserve some little of the true oyster flavor, church stews tasted of nothing but warm water and butter. Attempts were made by liberal and public-spirited church fioccers from time to time to time to remedy this fault by adding to church stews various flavoring extracts, the most popular of which was "Smith's Ecclesiastical Oyster Essence." The attempts, however, were uniformly failures. The flavor extracts did not plausibly imitate the flavor of the oyster, and in many instances complaints were made that the church cooks had mixed ham or onions with their oysters, and that they were simply bringing disgrace upon a sacred cause.

The invention of the church festival spoon at once put a stop to all complaint. This spoon, as every one now knows, is impregnated so thoroughly with the flavor of the oyster that the person who uses it in connection with any sort of food tastes nothing but the pure oyster flavor. During the past winter those church festivals at which the ingenious spoon was used were able totally to discard oysters. Their oyster stews were made of nothing but warm water, a little oleomargarine, and a sprinkling of salt and pepper, but when they were eaten with the church spoon the customers agreed with one voice that they had never tasted more delicious oyster stews in the whole course of their lives. The festival managers were thus enabled to save the cost of two or three quartes of oysters and to give complete satisfaction to the public—a state of things without a parallel in the memory of the oldest and most pious inhabitant.

It was obvious that the conception of a flavored spoon need not be confined to the narrow field of oysters. The soups prepared at most of our city restaurants bear a close relation to church festival stews in their composition. They are made upon a basis of warm water and oleomargarine, to which a few grains of rice, a few sticks of vermicelli, or a scrap of bone are added according to the style of soup ordered by the customer. In point of flavor they are all precisely alike, having nothing whatever except such as is communicated by pepper and salt. Now, the adaptation of the idea of the church festival spoon to purely secular soups was inevitable as soon as the success of the original spoon was established. The public will, therefore, hardly be surprised to learn that a complete set of flavoring spoons, designed for the general market, has just been manufactured by a well-known chemist.

In restaurants where these spoons are used all soup will consist of nothing but warm water with enough oleomargarine to furnish a slight greasy surface. The customer may order any one of the twenty-five varieties of soup for which flavoring spoons have so far been devised, and he will receive in every instance precisely the same soup. Nevertheless, with the aid of the flavoring spoon, he will enjoy what to his palate will present itself as the sort of soup which he had ordered. The simplicity and cheapness of this system will be apparent at a glance, and it is thought that the receipts of an average down town restaurant will be increased at least 30 per cent. by the use of the new flavoring spoons.

Undoubtedly the grand idea of imprisoning flavor in a spoon instead of an article of food is susceptible of still further expansion. We may yet be able to convert potatoes into a dozen different vegetables—so far as taste is concerned—by using flavoring spoons, and the system may even be applied to beverages. Certainly, the church festival spoon was one of the grandest ideas of the age, and we may yet sit down to a gorgeous banquet the variety and charm of which will consist entirely in the careful selection and arrangement of flavoring spoons.

Confessing a Murder for Watch Two Innocent Men Were Hanged.

In March Bill Ludlow and Al Weissinger were privately executed at Selma, Ala., for the killing of Mr. Weissinger, and their guilt (although up to the last moment they strongly asserted their innocence) was not questioned by anyone, so conclusive was the evidence against them. Since the hanging matters on the Weissinger plantations have not been "altogether lovely," as it was believed by many white people, which belief was largely shared by negroes, that there were three besides the two who were hanged concerned in the crime, and threats were freely made that it would go hard with anyone who had assisted at the tragedy. Last Wednesday afternoon Henry Ivy, who has been haunted by thoughts of the execution and was suffering from pangs of conscience, made a clear confession of the crime, pronouncing himself as the man who really did the killing, and implicating his brother, Porter Ivy, who received a life sentence for his share in the crime, and Tim Acoff, who was then at large on the plantation. The confession was made without fear or compulsion to seven intelligent white men. How the Lawless Mob Was Received at Catlettsburg—The Escape of the Military with the Prisoners—The Pursuit and Battle at Ash-land—Major Allen's Account.
CINCINNATI, November 2.—The Granite State, the steam boat that yesterday carried the prisoners Neal and Craft from Catlettsburg to Maysville, reached here this morning. Her officers state that the boat was taken into the service of the State by Major Allen and commanded to make no landing except at Portsmouth. They did not land even at Portsmouth, and reached Maysville at 2 A. M., where there was no excitement, there being no news of the trouble. The prisoners who had been carefully kept in one of the rooms at the end of the cabin, were transferred to the jail, and the officers know nothing more about them. They say the pilot house and all the upper part of the boat show bullet marks, but that only two men and a roustabout were injured by the fire of the men on the ferry boat. One of these was a drummer, who was hit on the hand. The other was a soldier who was struck on the head. The wounds are not serious.

The Captain of the Granite State says that Major Allen engaged their steamer on Tuesday night to convey the prisoners and troops to Maysville, but this was kept a profound secret even from the other boat officers.

Major Allen wishing to avoid a collision with the mob, they telegraphed to Major Allen that they would be at Catlettsburg at half-past eleven but failed to reach there till afternoon. He thinks that if they could have arrived promptly the whole trouble would have been avoided. When the boat came to Catlettsburg there were ominious signs of a disturbance. Prominent men at that place assured Capt. Kirker that the boat would be attacked. A large shipment of cattle was kept off for fear of disaster. A committee from the Ashland mob waited on Major Allen, and demanded the prisoners. The demand was, of course, refused, and the committee warned Major Allen that the prisoners would be taken.

When the boat left Catlettsburg, the mob took the train, which consisted of an engine, a passenger car and four flat cars. The train was filled with men, and as the road runs near the river at the start, the man could be heard hollowing, and could be seen firing at the boat. The distance was too great to make this of any other significance than defiance or threatening. When Ashland was reached the ferryboat was seen, apparently filled with belligerant people, and the wharfboat was also full of men and the banks lined with people. The pilot blew two whistles, as if to land, but with no intention of landing. This was a ruse to get away from the ferryboat. When the latter saw the Granite State was steaming by, four whistles were sounded by the ferryboat to get the Granite State to land. No attention was paid to it, and then the firing began. The Granite State refused to take the prisoners until a written order was issued commanding them to do so. Brose Dennis, who, with Mr. Williamson, occupied the pilot house, the latter being on watch, says that two soldiers were placed in the pilot house to keep the pilots at their post. He says that shots were fired at the Granite State both from the wharf boat and from the mob on the bank. Many of these were aimed at the pilot house, and six balls struck the pilot house. A number of other bullet marks appear on other parts of the boat. Of the firing from the bank and wharf boat, Dennis is certain. Both he and Clerk Fisher say that it would have been easy for the ferry boat to have overtaken them, and had a renewal of the battle if the troops had not acted with promptness in returning the fire. They speak in commendation of the action of the officers, and say there was no disposition shown to be bloodthirsty or malicious.

ASHLAND, Ky., Nov, 3, 1882.—Neal and Craft were granted a change of venue by Judge Brown to Carter county, on Tuesday. They were taken by the military at Catlettsburg aboard the Granite State. After the prisoners were put aboard the boat the streets leading to the landing were guarded by soldiers to prevent any attempt to rescue them. While in this situation a large number of men arrived from Ashland and appointed a committee to wait on Major Allen to demand the delivery of the prisoners to them. This the Major politely declined and ordered his men aboard the boat. The men from Ashland and a large number from Catlettsburg then boarded the train and left about the time the boat rounded out and arrived at Ashland ahead of her. There must have been five or six hundred men and boys on the train.

Several thousand persons had assembled on Front street, men, women and children to see the boat as she passed the city. Very little time elapsed before she rounded the point and as she came in full view of the landing, it was apparent that the soldiers apprehended an attack and were prepared for any that might be made. The crowd on the landing were greatly excited. There being no other boat at the wharf the ferryboat was boarded by from thirty to fifty men and boys, some of them armed with guns. The boat was headed for the Granite State. After the head of the boat was out toward the Ohio shore, some one on her hailed the steamer by waving a handkercheif, but she kept ahead of the ferryboat, all the time approaching her, and when about seventy-five yards from the Granite State a fire was opened on her by those on the ferryboat which was immediately returned by the soldiery. Several persons on the ferryboat were slightly wounded, one of whom James McDonald has since died. The worst work was done among the citizens who were taking no hand in the matter, but were merely on Front street as spectators. The firing among the citizens was most wanton and unprovoked.

"Was it lively?" said a passenger who came down on the Granite State, "well, it just was. It was like running a blockade during the war; the people were crazy."

"Tell us your experience."

"Well, it was an experience I want to shun next time. When the boat landed at Catlettsburg stages were run out as usual, the crew having no idea of a disturbance. The Captain was on the roof directing his crew, and afterwards went below to talk to a hog shipper. The first thing he knew a file of soldiers, comprising two companies, marched down the bank and took up a position on the boat's forecastle. The prisoners (Neal and Craft) were taken on board, and three companies remained on shore to keep back the crowd of people who followed the procession.

The commander of the brigade just took charge of the boat in regular military style, and she was regularly pressed into service, correct documents being served on the captain. If the crowd had made a demonstration then it would have been a terrible affair and no mistake. The boat backed out without any trouble, and shortly we saw the mob chasing the boat in a train of cars on shore. Angry fists were shook from the car windows, and shots were frequently fired by the mob, but the boat was too far out in the river to be touched. When Ashland was reached, and the ferryboat was seen to be in possession of the mob, the soldiers were drawn up on the roof, the guards and the lower decks. On the roof the soldiers on the left hand side of the boat were flat on their stomachs, and on the right hand side, below the skylights, another file was ranged. The first shot was fired by the mob, when several more followed. Then it was the soldiers let go. There was a whole volley fired, being mainly directed to the pilot house of the ferryboat. That is one reason why so many bullets reached the shore, although some inexperienced hands had hold of rifles, which were fired at random.

"By—I saw a fellow step boldly out on the deck of the ferryboat, take deliberate aim at our pilot and fire. The aim was so close that it splintered the windowsill of the pilot house. That pilot was a plucky fellow. He just threw open the sashes, remarking that he didn't want glass in his, and gave them a full unobstructed view of his person, coolly performing the duty of his watch. I believe his name is Brose Dennis.

"That made the soldiers mad and they let go. That shot aimed at our pilot was one of the first fired by the mob.

"Our pilot's conduct was strongly in contrast with the fellow on the ferryboat. When the first volley from the soldiers riddled his box he let go of the wheel and fell back. Then he jumped up and fell over again going through the sash to the deck below. How he escaped was a sort of a miracle, but I heard he was only hurt in the hand.

ASHLAND, Ky., November 4.—Another day of gloom. Flags are still at half-mast and the city heavily draped. Alex. Harris' funeral services were held to-day at the Presbyterian Church. He died yesterday morning. His death-bed scene was most touching, calling his friends about him, bidding them farewell, and cheering his grief-stricken wife to the last. A tremendous crowd gathered at the church to-day, and, after the most solemn and impressive ceremonies, followed the body to the last resting place. Mr. Harris was a young man, about thirty years of age, leaving a young wife and one child to mourn his loss.

For the last twenty-four hours the parents and friends of little Willie Terrie, fourteen years of age, who was wounded in the knee, have been trying to induce him to permit the doctors to amputate his leg, but the heroic little fellow says he is not afraid to die, and prefers death to being a cripple for life. Poor boy, little does he know that death is so near, for while the doctors were endeavoring to prepare his system for the operation, gangrene has set in, and his case is hopeless.

Another case that excites much sympathy in many kind hearts, who administer to his wants, is that of Robert Lawther, who suffers intense pain, and whose death is expected at any moment.

Mrs. Terrie, wounded in the breast, is the next worse case. She is nursing an infant, and her recovery is thought to be doubtful.

The balance of the wounded, so far as we have been able to learn, are doing well, though doctors inform us that a serious change for the worse may take place at any moment in the condition of several of the patients.

The Coroner's jury convened at 2 o'clock this afternoon. The evidence of several witnesses on the stand seem to shed some light upon the infamous conduct of the soldiers. Captain Kirker, of the Granite State, being placed under oath testified as follows:

Several shots were fired from the train between Ashland and Catlettsburg at the steamer, but they fell short; that when approaching Ashland he saw a large crowd of men, women and children gathered on the bank, and that he could see no arms of any kind, or any demonstration whatever towards harming the boat; that when about opposite the wharf he noticed the ferryboat putting out into the stream, and not until then did he apprehend an attack being made, nor would he, had the troops been under his command, have thought an order to fire justifiable. He states, according to his best judgment, that the crowd on the ferryboat did not exceed twenty or twenty-five. He says that after the first volley from the troops their firing should have ceased, and that he did all in his power to make them desist, and he knew that they were destroying the lives of innocent people. He does not know the exact number of shots fired by the soldiers, but overheard three of the men saying one had shot four, one six and another seven. He says the soldiers on the way down were laughing and singing in a boisterous manner, and that he rebuked them for acting so after such wanton destruction of human life.

The next witness was Mr. I. C. Nelson, Express Messenger of the Granite State. He testified that the mob on the ferryboat did not exceed twenty-five, nor did he at any time apprehend any danger from their attack calling forth an order to fire by the soldiers; that he, with others, hunted over the boat for bullet holes, and six were all he could find, two of which were evidently caused by shots from the soldiers. The only wounded he saw was a soldier who had a shot under the scalp, which was easily picked out, and a drummer boy who had one of his drum-sticks broken in his hand, from which he received a scratch, but no injury from the bullet. He, like Captain Kirker, thinks that after the first volley, the balance of the shooting was uncalled for. He saw no shots from the shore or the crowd on the bank.

Ham. Davisson, proprietor of the Ashland and Ironton hack line, was next sworn. He was waiting on the Ohio side for his regular hour to start with his hack to Ironton, and noticed a large crowd of men, women and children on the Kentucky shore. He saw the Granite State come in sight, and noticed the ferryboat leave her landing with a number of men and boys which he considered would be a good hackload. He heard two shots fired, but couldn't tell whether from the ferryboat or wharfboat. A volley from the soldiers followed immediately. He saw steam rushing from the ferryboat, and thought her to be on fire. His horses took fright and having to quiet them, he failed to see anything else, except that a soldier, after the firing had ceased, stepped out of the pilot house and fired a shot in the direction of the town; didn't see any shooting from the Ohio shore, nor arms in the hands of any one standing around.

John Kouns, Sheriff of Boyd county, sworn. He said he did not consider the troops necessary to protect the prisoners. He had selected his men to accompany him to bring them back, when orders were given him to request the guards.

Several other witnesses were sworn, giving testimony of minor importance.

The jury adjourned at 5 p. m., indefinitely, as important witnesses are yet to be heard from.

AshLAND, KENTUCKY, November 1.

To-day has closed the saddest that has ever dawned in the history of Ashland. The murderers, Craft and Neal, have added additional sorrow and suffering to this outraged people. This noon about twenty-five boys and men, some of whom were in various stages of intoxication, seized the switch engine of the A. C. and I. R. R. and a coach belonging to the S. V. Road, and went to Catlettsburg after the prisoners, very much against the wishes and judgment of the practical and sensible part of the community, who last night gave up all hopes of getting the murderers away from the soldiers on account of the strength of the latter and the superiority of their arms. No demonstration were made by this crowd, however, in Catlettsburg, and the soldiers succeeded in getting the prisoners aboard the steamer, Granite State, about 3 p. m., without any offer of interruption being made.

The crowd on the train, however, started back to Ashland, where they arrived ahead of the boat; and about twenty boys ran down and seized the ferryboat. put a pistol to the Captain's head and commanded him to put out in the stream to intercept the Granite State. The ferryboat is a slow tub, and their efforts were plainly fruitless from the start. Unluckily some foolish fellow on the ferryboat, to the sorrow of many homes in Ashland to-night, discharged a small 22-caliber revolver. The soldiers immediately oponed fire with a heavy volley on this handful of boys, completely riddling the boat with balls, one of which struck the bolts in the man-head of the boiler, and immediately the escape of scalding steam was added to the rain of bullets, disabling the craft and making the condition of the occupants truly pitiable, though this was probably their just deserts for their foolhardiness, which meets with the disapproval of the entire community, who probably would not have felt any indignation towards the soldiers had they confined their unrelenting fire strictly towards the ferryboat, which was the only point of attack.

Almost the entire town had assembled on top of the river bank, in windows and balconies all along the river front, from motives of curiosity, having heard the prisoners were coming on the Granite State. The soldiers, after disabling the ill-fated craft, directed their fire into the crowd assembled on the bank, literally fulfilling Governor Blackburn's boast that he would kill every man, woman and child of Boyd County if necessary to defend these murderers.

At the first fire of the soldiers the people on the banks began to hunt cover from stray bullets, which move on their part seemed to draw the attention of the soldiers from the ferryboat to them with results that were most disastrous; for while there were only three persons wounded on the ferryboat, the list of killed and wounded, men, women and children, on the bank and in houses, were twenty-four in number. last week:

PARIS, KY., Nov. 2, 1882.—8:25 P.M.
To Governor L. P. Blackburn:
At twelve o'clock, November 1, our command marched to the river front at Catlettsburg, to await the arrival of a boat to convey us home. We marched the prisoners, Neal and Craft, with two companies as guards, into the wharf boat, and left the remaining companies at the top of the hill, to repulse an attack which we anticipated from an Ashland mob. A few minutes after we took our position a train of cars consisting of one locomotive, one passenger and five flat cars closely packed with a mob from Ashland, Ky., arrived; a delegation from the mob waited on me, and demanded the prisoners Neal and Craft, threatening that if we did not surrender them peaceably they would use force. Their demand was peremptorily refused. They then informed us that they would attack us as our boat passed Ashland with a force of at least two thousand men, supported by a ferry boat with a battery of four pieces of artillery. We then withdrew to our boat, the Granite State, and started down the river. The mob at the same time took their train and headed toward Ashland. The train ran along the river bank about a mile at the same speed as our boat, and just before leaving the river opened fire on us. A great number of the mob fired on us, but our troops, with great coolness and self restraint did not return the fire, although the bullets of the mob struck in the water all about the boat. As we got nearly opposite Ashland a ferry boat, closely packed with armed men, left the shore and headed toward us, and signaled for us to stop. As we paid no attention to their signals they commenced firing on us with rapidity. After they had fired two or three volleys and had wounded two of our men, the order was given for our troops to fire, which they did, and a very spirited engagement ensued, in which the mob was badly crippled. Though our cannon was on deck, and finely handled by Lieutenant Blygh and his men, I did not deem it necessary to fire it, as our infantry was sufficient to repulse the attack. We had five men wounded or hurt in the engagement, but none seriously. The troops acted with admirable bravery, coolness, and self-possession. We will reach Lexington this morning at 9 o'clock.

JOHN R. ALLEN,
Major Commanding.

A Penitentiary in a State of Siege.

JERSEY CITY, September 10th.—The Penitentiary at Snake Hill is in a state of siege. Rival Wardens claim possession. Warden Meehan, who holds the fort, has closed the gates, and no person can enter nor leave. Warden Bownes secured a warrant for the arrest of Meehan, but it cannot be served. A number of constables determined to day to effect an entrance to arrest Meehan and take possession for Bownes, but one of them used a telephone to inform the men holding the Penitentiary, and the plan failed. When the gates were closed, one prisoner, the mail carrier, was outside the walls of the Penitentiary, and there he is still.

The Pittsburg Labor Situation.

PITTSBURG, September 10th.—The men are rapidly breaking away from the Amalgamated Association, and within the next forty-eight hours a number of mills will be in operation in this district with Union men who have signified a desire to return to work without signing the scale, and at last year's rates. Among the mills which will resume are those of Graff, Bennett & Co., Everson, Macrum & Co., Henry Lloyd & Son, and Brown & Co., in Pittsburgh; Russ Bros. & Co., of Newcastle, Pa., and Brown, Bonnell & Co., in Youngstown. Of these, Graff, Bennett & Co., and Russ Bros. & Co., will resume tomorrow, the balance on Tuesday. Graff, Bennett & Co., will start their sheet department, Everson, Macrum & Co., their sheet mill, Lloyd & Sons one car mill, Brown & Co. the rail mill. The other departments will resume as soon as possible.

Colorado Greenbackers.

DENVER, September 10th.—The Greenback State Convention yesterday nominated Geo. W. War for Governor, F. O. Saunders for Lieutenant-Governor, and L. J. Hersinger for Secretary of State. The Convention was bitter and strong, on account of the fight over the prohibition question. The prohibition clause was finally adopted.

Two Attempts at Suicide.

CHICAGO, September 10th.—A young woman, claiming to be a niece of Rose Conkling, has twice tried to commit suicide in the past forty-eight hours, but ineffectually. She says the stony heart of her distinguished relative in refusing to aid her to get a position is the cause of her attempts. Her story is not much credited.

CHICAGO, September 10th.—A Times special says: A masked mob from the country gathered at Washington, Ind., early this morning, with the intention of lynching John Hunter, who murdered William Lents. The Sheriff had quietly garrisoned the jail with thirty armed men. The vigilantes displaced the ropes of the fire and police bells, fired volleys to frighten the citizens, and sent fifty men over the jail fence. Three attempts to force the doors were unavailing, and the appeals of the Sheriff and Prosecuting Attorney caused the mob to disperse. Hunter lay crouched in his cell all day.

ALL AROUND THE GLOBE.

J. L. Browne has been appointed postmaster at Wamego, Kas.

After October 1st the East Saginaw, Mich., postoffice will be a free delivery office.

Yesterday was the hottest day of the season in Chicago. Good weather for corn, which is improving rapidly.

The Kansas Greenbackers yesterday nominated for governor Ex-Gov. Chas. Robinson, the first governor of Kansas.

The supreme court of California has decided that the election of city officers must be held this year at the same time as the general state election.

The Texas cattle fever has made its appearance in the vicinity of Auburn, N. Y. Twenty-five domestic cattle have died and a large number are sick.

Michigan millers complain of the bad quality of new wheat which has been more injured by wet weather in the southern section than the farmers acknowledge.

The first bale of cotton received at Louisville this season was sold at the board of trade yesterday for 30 cents a pound, middlings. It came from West Umpka, Ala.

At Bangor, Me., yesterday, the jury in the case of Mary Glinn, on trial for the murder of her daughter's illegitimate child, gave a verdict of murder in the first degree.

James B. Shirk, mail agent on the Vandalia line, fell out of the door of a postal car while the train was running rapidly and was killed, near Indianapolis, Ind., yesterday.

The man Smith, who attempted on Monday to outrage a white lady in the vicinity of Little Rock, was yesterday killed by a disguised party, who shot him to death.

Over one hundred women are on trial at Gross Beeskerck, Hungary, charged with poisoning their husbands. The guilt of thirty-five of the women has been proven.

Gen. Sherman stated during his last visit to St. Louis that it is his intention to leave the army before the law retiring him goes into effect and that he will return to St. Louis to live.

The roof of the Erdway elevator in Buffalo was yesterday blown off by an explosion. Cause unknown. The building burned to the ground. Three men were burned. The loss is $250,000.

Wm. Sexton, the billardist of New York city, sues the Bleecker Street Railway company for $5,000 for injuries sustained when ejecting him from a car for refusing to pay his fare a second time.

J. B. Kelsey, a private banker at Versailles, Mo., was arrested at Tipton, Mo., yesterday, charged with misappropriating funds deposited in his bank, which closed its doors Wednesday. Liabilities of bank $40,000.

A. Goodrich, employed by the Cunard company, was severely beaten by the striking longshore men Wednesday night in Boston. Three loads of Italians arrived yesterday morning. The strikers offered no violence.

At Paterson, N. J., yesterday, the coroner's jury found James Kennedy guilty of manslaughter for neglecting his children while sick with the small-pox. He locked them in the garret and did not provide medical attendance.

Maj. Chas. H. Cole, of Dallas, Tex., died suddenly at Austin Wednesday night. He has been identified with Texas railroads, immigration, land and other enterprises since the war and was well known throughout the country.

Alex. Julian, brother of Hon. Ira Julian, committed suicide on the fair grounds at Louisville, Ky., yesterday, by shooting himself through the brain. He was a candidate for sheriff in the late election and his defeat is believed to be the cause.

Rev. Leander Streber, better known as "Father Leander," in charge of St. Marion Roman Catholic church, and an old citizen of Louisville, died at his home yesterday. He was born in Bavaria and came to this country in 1844, and to Louisville in 1846.

Judge W. D. Kelley, of Pennsylvania, addressed a large audience in the eastern hall of the exposition building, Denver, Col., Wednesday night, on the growth of Colorado for the last ten years, and the reduction of the internal revenue tax. It was a masterly effort.

An exciting horse thief hunt is progressing in Van Buren county, Ark. Two thieves were killed on the 22d, and one has been sent to the penitentiary for sixteen years. The thieves are a band of desperate characters and it is anticipated that there will be trouble in their capture.

C. B. Hawley, L. V. Grimes and Cicero Grimes, the Arizona murderers, last night made a full confession of the manner in which they murdered Hall and Vail. Later Hawley and L. V. Grimes were quietly and expeditiously lynched. Cicero Grimes was taken to a place of safety.

A new railroad company has been organized with Norvin Green at the head, called the "Great American and European Short Railroad company." Its object is to shorten the trip to Europe by conveying passengers by rail to the eastern coast of Newfoundland and thence shipping them to the west coast of Ireland. Three or four days will thus be saved.

Some excitement has been caused in the jewelry trade in St. John, N. B., by customs officers visiting four establishments and seizing large quantities of American jewelry. It is claimed that only a small portion of imported jewelry paid the duty. The goods are smuggled into the upper provinces, it is said, and then sent to St. John with regular invoices.

Last Monday at noon news to the effect that the pack train had been taken in on the Pioneer trail, and the express messenger, Andy Hall, of Florence, and Dr. Vail, of Globe, had been killed. But the telegraph wire had been cut by the robbers and only vague rumors of the tragedy could be obtained. For four days the air was rife with conflicting reports of the affair and not till Sheriff Gabriel returned Thursday evening, did we get the particulars. Sheriff Gabriel was at Silver King when the news reached him, and he started at once for Globe, arriving there at eleven o'clock that evening. He found the whole town in arms and almost beside themselves with excitement. They had brought in both bodies and burried them, and were making earnest but disorganized efforts to discover and capture the robbers. As is usual on such occasions every man had a suggestion to offer but no one seemed to understand exactly what to do. Mr. Gabriel, in his capacity of deputy United States Marshal, took hold of the case and began a search for a clue. He asked Capt. D. B. Lacy if any one in Globe was suspicioned, and the latter replied, "Yes, I suspicion young Grimes. He belongs to my company of rangers and during the Indian excitements was first to answer the call to arms, but on this occasion has kept away, and did not even come to see the bodies when they were brought in." Mr. Gabriel went to work on this clue and at the end of hour's careful investigation went back to Lacy and told him that young Grimes was undoubtedly one of the men and should be secured at once. They then ascertained that the latter had gone down to the Wheat Fields, nine miles from Globe to work on the grade. They left immediately for that point, and on reaching the ground got Lindsay Lewis to go up to the grade and bring Grimes down to the house. Lacy and Lewis questioned the prisoner closely but he denied his connection with the crime with the utmost sang froid, and they were about to give up the case when Marshal Gabriel, who had been arrested and confessed that he was in town when the prisoner on his phone, he was on the hill and saw him shoot at Hall three times." This sudden charge threw the prisoner off his guard, and he at once exclaimed, "No, I didn't, I only shot at him twice." Seeing he was caught Grimes confessed the whole thing and stated that a man by the name of Hawley was his partner in the crime, but denied that his brother had any knowledge of it. Messrs. Gabriel, Lacy and Lewis then took Grimes up to the mill, about five miles from Globe, and Lewis guarded him there while the others went to town to capture Hawley. In the mean time Marshal Gabriel had, by a little sharp practice, made Grimes believe that his brother had been arrested and confessed to having had a hand in the crime and then the prisoner owned that the elder Grimes and Hawley planned the robbery. When Gabriel arrived in town he went to Grimes' house three times but did not find the old man in, so he then turned his attention to Hawley, and after some trouble in finding his house, captured the murderer. A number of citizens protested that Hawley could not be the right man as two men were willing to swear that he was in town when the robbery occurred, and demanded the officers warrant. Mr. Gabriel quieted their objections by saying that he had arrested the prisoner on another charge. Mr. Gabriel's next move was to go to the mill, get young Grimes and take the two prisoners over to Saxe's ranch, about 8 miles from Globe on the King trail. He knew if he kept the prisoners in town and the citizens found out they were the robbers they would be lynched at once, and he desired, if possible, to get them to tell all about the robbery and the whereabouts of the treasure before the citizens could get hold of them.

They acknowledged the robbery of the Wells, Fargo & Co.'s treasure chest containing $5,000 in gold coin, and the killing of Andy Hall, one of the most trusty of the company's messengers, and who has a very favorable record as one of Powell's men, who some years ago explored the Colorado canon. As soon as it became known that the men were in town, a large meeting took place at the jail, and after considerable parley between the officers and the people, the prisoners were and surrounded and taken to Dr. Stallo's hall, where a court of inquiry was organized and a full hearing had. It was decided to hang them without delay. The prisoners asked for three hours time and promised to reveal the place of the money stolen. This was acceded and they, in company with about thirty citizens, repaired to the foot hills of the Pinal mountains, about four miles from town; and there pointed out the hiding place of the money, and most of it was found and taken in charge by Mr. Vosburgh, agent of the express company at this place. DALLAS, TEXAS, March 20.—Tuscan Langler, and a man in his employ, named Harrison, were arrested at Langler's residence on a charge of killing A. H. Crooks and S. J. Jory, by a posse of citizens, and turned over to the deputy sheriff. After reaching the hotel, a party of masked men overpowered the guard and shot Langler dead, and Harrison was hanged to the trestle works of a bridge. None of the perpetrators have been identified, and nothing has been ascertained to implicate Harrison in the murder of Crooks and Jory, and his only offense seems to have been that he was in Langler's employ.

A HORRIBLE TRAGEDY.
Two Men Killed While at Work.
A private letter from Prineville, addressed to us by Joseph Henkle, contains the sad information that Aron Crooks and his son-in-law Jorly, were shot and killed while peacebly and quietly at work near that place, by one F. T. Langdon. The difficulty is supposed to have arrisen from a dispute over a piece of land. Crooks is a son of the Hon. Crooks of Linn county.

LATER.

Since receiving the above, an exchange says that Langdon was taken from the custody of a deputy sheriff at Prineville by a mob who opened fire upon and killed him. Mr. Harrison, a man in the employ of Langdon, who was also arrested at the same time with the latter at the latter's residence was also taken possession of by the mob and hanged. Nothing was known to implicate Harrison in the crime.

Robert Bailey, teacher in a schoo near Red Bud Illinois, was stabbed to death on Saturday, by a James E. McBride, a seventeen-year-old pupil, whom he was attempting to chastise for breach of discipline. McBride was arrested and held in $5000 bail to await the action of the Grand Jury.

The University Club House, 1316 Walnut street, Phila., Pa., was formally opened on Saturday. Bishop Stevens, the President, and others making addresses. The club is purely social, and it is requisite that a member shall be a college graduate.

Edward E. Blanchard, aged 29 years, Assistant Teller of the Farmers and Mechanics' National Bank of Buffalo, disappeared about a week ago, with money belonging to the bank. Wine, women and gambling caused his ruin.

A sub-committee of the House Committee on Territories unanimously agreed on Saturday to report favorably to the full committee the bill for the establishment of the Territory of North Dakota, and providing a temporary government therefor.

George Payne, well known to visitors of museums throughout the United States as "the man without arms," died last Thursday at his home in Williamsburg, New York, aged 27 years. From his birth he was compelled to make his legs and toes go service for arms and hands, and he fed himself like other people. He also shaved himself and was a good penman. He leaves a wife and child.

Number one of volume one of the Wickliffe Tribune has reached this office. It is a six column folio, published weekly by Mr. H. F. Thurman. It has a much better appearance than country papers usually have. It is welcomed to THE BULLETIN's exchange table and deserves to prosper.

The sewer crossing Fourteenth street, on the east side of Poplar, has caved in, causing a hole near the centre of the street of about three feet deep and four feet in diameter. It has been baricaded, however, to avoid accidents and will doubtless be filled up and the sewer repaired as soon as the weather will permit.

—A lady named Mrs. Dennis O'Brien, living in the Clark block, on Ohio levee, died yesterday about noon, and will be taken to Grand Chain for burial to-day. She was the mother of a numerous family of children, one of whom is employed as "devil" in THE BULLETIN composing-room.

—A white man named Jacob McEwen and a negro were out in a canoe on the back water, just below Belmont, on Wednesday, and, in an unguarded moment they lost their balance, turned the canoe over, and the white man was drowned. The negro saved himself by clinging to the overturned canoe until help came to him.

—One thousand dollars worth of mules, belonging to Mr. Frank Crossno, a Mississippi county, Mo., farmer, died from the effects of being driven through cold back water a day or two ago. They were on a ridge surrounded by water, and Mr. Crossno drove them through the water to his stables with the result as stated.

—The Illinois Central railroad has a large force of men constantly at work in the railroad yards, repairing the company's tracks. Continued wet weather has had an injurious effect upon the ties and much traffic has done upon the same for the rails, hence the urgent necessity for extensive repairs.

—An item is going the rounds to the effect that a fortune-teller drove a woman crazy in Buffalo, N. Y., the other day. Not for the sake of the fortune-teller profession, but for the sake of truth, we feel like starting the suspicion that the woman was crazy before she went to the clairvoyant's house. She must have been.

Maude attempted to cross over the made land on the Mississippi side of Cairo yesterday morning into the channel, but when she reached a point about opposite the slaughter houses, she ran aground right in a corn field. All the power of her mighty engines was not equal to the task of pulling her off again, and the Port Eads went to her assistance and drew her off.

The town of Sparta is a red-hot temperance town, where the sale of liquor is prohibited by act of the town board, and the temperance people of the place are exceeding wroth at the audacity of the "two new saloon keepers," as the Sparta Plain-dealer calls them. A number of cities in this state have increased the amount of yearly saloon licenses in order to raise more money for the necessities of the municipal government. The idea seems to be constantly spreading, too. Chicago started the ball and a number of smaller towns in southern and central Illinois took it up. The latest agitation of the matter is in Springfield, where the Journal urges the propriety of raising the saloon license in order to meet the expense of improving streets etc.

Mr. C. H. Warner, of the Quincy, (Ill.), telephone exchange assumed charge of the Cairo telephone exchange yesterday morning, relieving Mr. R. P. Hotchkiss, who has had the management of the latter for some time past and given general satisfaction. Mr. Warner is an old telegraph man and an experienced electrician, who has been connected with the management of telephones ever since their invention. Mr. Hotchkiss will be made superintendent of telephones of the southern portion of Illinois, with headquarters at Springfield.

Two houses floated by the city in the Ohio river yesterday morning about nine o'clock. But little more than the roofs were visible. They were small houses, not worth above fifty dollars when new; but tears of commiseration filled the eyes of tender hearted spectators on the levee, at the sad thought that the best business and residence portion of Paducah was being thus little by little carried down the remorseless stream, leaving the poor inhabitants no alternative but to get astride of a plank and come to Cairo for refuge.

Mayor Harrison, of Chicago, issued an order the other day that all gambling houses should close Saturday night at 7 o'clock. The object of this was not to trouble the gamblers, but to protect the wages of the working classes from the keno fiend and faro sharp. Promptly at the hour named last Saturday night the police served these notices and the gamblers without exception closed up. The thing worked like a charm, because the gamblers didn't resist. The gamblers say they don't object. They don't want the money of working-men. They want customers with more fat in them. Hereafter the rule will be enforced every Saturday. Nothing is said about the rest of the week, but the inference is that the houses are not to be molested as long as they allow the good wives to have the first shy at the weekly salaries of clerks and laborers.

The managers did not go on to London to fill the engagement, but camped for the day, and returned to Lebanon to show Monday.

nick-hathaway-carlisle-1882-10.A7: In all ages, except when the world was too young to wear shoes, people have had trouble with corns. The emperor Maximus, although he only wore shingles tied to his feet, declared that if it were not for corns he would be happy, and Alexander the Great said that a quack corn doctor was worse than the township politician. The other night during a dance at Carlisle, Ky., a negro named George Hathaway stepped on a corn belonging to a white man named Martin Murphy. Hathaway asked pardon, but there is no pardon for a man who puts an agricultural heel on a corn, and Murphy, entertaining this view, procured a pistol and shot the unfortunate Hathaway, killing him almost instantly. The courts will no doubt deal gently with the murderer, for every Kentucky juryman has a corn.

On a small island near Fiji a soft material is found, which on exposure, hardens and looks much like firebrick.

Immigration is pouring into the northwestern portion of Arkansas at a greater rate than ever known before.

Within the last year there were completed 1,641 miles of railroad in Texas, at an estimated cost for construction and equipment of $14,525,000.

A mock philanthropist has been sent to prison for a year from Englewood, Illinois. He had run an institution for feeble-minded children without children, but with profit to himself.

There are peers in the house of lords over eighty—Lord Shadbroke, who is 88; Lord Eversley, 88; Lord Mostyn, 87; Lord Wemyss, 86, and Lord Albemarle, 83. It is the fashion to picture the house of lords as a body of feeble old men. The greater majority are under 60, with a contingent under 30.

THE SMALL-POX IN BEDFORD—THE LATE RAIL-ROAD ACCIDENT—ABOUT MANUFACTORIES—DEATHS—FRACAS—THE POST-OFFICE, &C.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

APRIL 4, 1882.

The small-pox has broken out anew in the Little Otter neighborhood, Bedford county, and Dr. J. A. Otey writes that considerable excitement prevails thereabout. There are five cases now in the family of Benjamin Towry—two of varioloid and three of confluent small-pox.

J. M. Keith, the brakeman on the Virginia Midland road, who had both legs severed Sunday night near McIvor's station, is reported in a critical condition this morning, and cannot, it is thought, survive through the day.

The exemption of manufactures from taxation for the period of eighteen years by the City Council is causing a great many inquiries to be made by capitalists from abroad, and the clerk is constantly sending out copies of the ordinance. It is hoped that this exemption will result in some material good to the town.

The remains of Mrs. S. Rosenberg, of New York, who died at the residence of her father, Mr. Max Guggenheimer, Sr., of this city, yesterday, were sent North in a special coach this morning. The deceased was of one of the first Israelite families in the country, was a person of great beauty, rare culture, and in the full flush of womanhood. Her death was peculiarly sad and distressing.

A party of dissipated young men were before the Mayor this morning charged with attacking the colored workmen on the Richmond and Alleghany railroad with stones. Several of them were fined. One of the party had his collar-bone broken by one of the negroes engaged in the affray, who was sent on for indictment by the grand jury.

There is universal complaint about the execrably-bad management at the post-office here. As soon as the new postmaster took possession he sought to strengthen his influence over the negroes by making a delivery clerk of one of their number. The result was almost intolerable confusion, and a general mixing up of everybody's mail with somebody else's. Murmurings ensued, and complaints appeared in public print. One of the most efficient clerks in the office refused the association of this son of Ham, and delay was added to confusion. However, fully aware of this state of affairs, and seemingly, and I believe deliberately, in defiance of public sentiment, the postmaster has inducted into office another "sabal son of Sahara," thus aggravating the cause of complaint. It is not a question of whether a negro or a white person distributes the malls, however; it is simply a question of whether the business and corresponding portion of the community is to be subjected to this abominable annoyance merely to gratify the spit of a stripling whom force of circumstances has made postmaster.

Mr. Robert J. Snead has been elected individual book-keeper at the Lynchburg National Bank in the place of Mr. B. Estes Vaughan, promoted.

Ex-Policeman M. C. Mays died Sunday night and was buried to-day.

George J. Rice, President of the Utica, Ithaca and Elmira Railroad, was arrested in New York on a charge of forgery, over-issue of stock and embezzlement. It is said there is a discrepancy in his accounts of from $60,-000 to $100,000. He resided near Elmira.
